expect:
Mastering: Plot A is likely to produce greater biomass because high light and CO₂ maximise the rate of photosynthesis and glucose production. Low nitrate will limit protein synthesis but plants can still photosynthesise and store starch. Plot B has less glucose production from lower light. Overall, the photosynthetic rate is the primary driver of biomass.
Secure: Plot A — more glucose made via photosynthesis due to high light and CO₂; nitrate shortage limits protein but not photosynthesis itself.
Developing: Plot A because it has more light and CO₂ for photosynthesis.
Emerging: Plot A because it has more light.
value:
Mastering: Plot B is likely to produce greater biomass. Nitrate ions supply the nitrogen used to build amino acids and proteins, including the enzymes that control photosynthesis, and chlorophyll contains nitrogen too. With little nitrate, Plot A cannot make enough chlorophyll or enzymes, so its rate of photosynthesis falls even though light and CO₂ are plentiful — nitrate is the resource in shortest supply. Plot B has the nitrate needed to build that machinery, so over a whole growing season its lower light intensity holds the rate back less than Plot A's nitrate shortage does.
Secure: Plot B — low nitrate in Plot A limits protein and chlorophyll production, so the rate of photosynthesis and growth fall despite the high light and CO₂.
Developing: Plot B, because plants need nitrate to grow and Plot A does not have enough.
Emerging: Plot B because it has more nitrate.
note: F15: the key said Plot A and claimed a nitrate shortage 'limits protein but not photosynthesis itself'. The lesson states a shortage of any resource limits growth regardless of light or CO2, and nitrogen shortage lowers chlorophyll and enzyme levels, so it lowers the rate itself. Rekeyed to Plot B.
